title: The Rebel of the Family
description: Published in 1880 and Linton's most searching novel of the woman question: a young woman who rebels against her family and finds that freedom has its own price.
plot_or_argument: Perdita Morley, a strong-willed girl of the upper middle class, rejects the marriage her family has planned and insists on earning her living as a journalist; the novel follows her affair with a married man, her ostracism, her illness and the compromise by which she makes her peace with the world she had defied.
historical_context: 1880: the London of the women's colleges and the new professional openings, the feminist debates in the periodical press, and Linton's own complicated position between feminism and anti-feminism.
literary_significance: The Rebel of the Family is the most interesting of Linton's novels and a key text of the 1880s debate on the New Woman: it takes the feminist case seriously and then tests it against experience, and it is far more ambivalent than the essays for which Linton was notorious.

title: The True History of Joshua Davidson
description: Published in 1872 and Linton's most original book: the life of a working-class carpenter who tries to live literally by the Sermon on the Mount in modern London.
plot_or_argument: Joshua Davidson, a Somerset carpenter and a member of a small sect, comes to London as a Christian Socialist, preaches the literal gospel to the poor, is hated by the churches and the respectable, and is killed by a mob during a bread riot — a modern repetition of the life of Christ.
historical_context: 1871-72: the Paris Commune, the London of the 1870s, the Christian Socialist movement and the Tichborne case, and the Victorian fascination with the 'historical Jesus'.
literary_significance: The True History of Joshua Davidson is one of the boldest religious novels of the century: its application of the gospel literally to Victorian London anticipated the Christian Socialism of the 1880s, and its scandalous success made Linton a figure of national controversy for the second time.

title: Under Which Lord?
description: Published in 1879 and Linton's most ambitious social novel: the conflict between a High Church squire and the Radical workman he has made his son-in-law.
plot_or_argument: Lorne, the young Radical poet whom the old squire has educated and married to his daughter, turns against his patron's Christianity and his class; the novel follows the marriage, the newspaper campaign, the strike and the ruin that the conflict brings on both families.
historical_context: 1878-79: the ritualist controversy in the Church of England, the agricultural labourers' unions, and the Radical press of the 1870s.
literary_significance: Under Which Lord? is one of the strongest English novels of class and religion in the 1870s: its portrait of a working-class intellectual and its analysis of the alliance between radicalism and unbelief make it a serious contribution to the condition-of-England tradition.

title: My Literary Life
description: Published in 1899 after her death and the frank memoir of the first woman to hold a salaried post on the London daily press.
plot_or_argument: Linton recalls her Cumberland childhood, her arrival in London in 1845, her work on the Morning Chronicle, the writers she knew — Dickens, Thackeray, Carlyle, Bulwer-Lytton — her unhappy marriage and her long career of fiction and journalism, and defends her opinions on women with undiminished pugnacity.
historical_context: 1898-99: the London press of the 1840s-90s, the world of the Victorian man and woman of letters, and the retrospect of a literary life at the end of the century.
literary_significance: My Literary Life is one of the most valuable Victorian literary memoirs and a central document in the history of women's journalism: it records, with unusual honesty, the professional life of a woman who spent fifty years in the London press.

title: Robert Elsmere
description: Published in 1888 and the central English novel of the Victorian crisis of faith: the story of a clergyman who loses his belief and finds a religion of social service.
plot_or_argument: Robert Elsmere, a young Oxford clergyman of the Broad Church school, falls in love with Catherine Leyburn, a woman of austere Evangelical faith; his reading of the German critics and his visit to the German universities destroy his belief in the resurrection, he resigns his living, and he founds a 'New Brotherhood' of social service in the East End, where he dies of overwork.
historical_context: 1888: the Broad Church and the Lux Mundi group, the higher criticism of the Bible, the university settlement movement, and the Oxford of T. H. Green and Arnold Toynbee.
literary_significance: Robert Elsmere was the most discussed novel of the 1880s and the central literary document of the Victorian religious crisis: it sold in enormous numbers, was preached against from pulpits across Britain and America, and its picture of the passage from faith to social service made it the representative novel of its decade.

title: Marcella
description: Published in 1894 and Ward's great novel of the New Woman and the land question: an heiress who refuses her class and must learn to work within it.
plot_or_argument: Marcella Boyce, brought up by a Radical father and educated as an artist, returns to the decaying family estate and falls in love with Aldous Raeburn, the heir of the neighbouring Tory landowner; she breaks off the engagement over a poaching case, trains as a nurse, and finally marries him to work for housing and rural reform from within.
historical_context: 1894: the agricultural depression and the land question, the London poor law and nursing reform, and the New Woman debate at its height.
literary_significance: Marcella is one of the most substantial New Woman novels and the finest English novel of the land question: its heroine's conversion from romantic Radicalism to practical social work made it a central text of the 1890s and it was read across the political spectrum.

title: Helbeck of Bannisdale
description: Published in 1898 and Ward's most concentrated tragedy: the love of an old Catholic squire and a young woman of the modern world, destroyed by their beliefs.
plot_or_argument: Alan Helbeck, the last of an ancient recusant family, falls in love with Laura Fountain, the daughter of a Cambridge sceptic; their love is destroyed by the conflict between his Catholicism and her inherited unbelief, and Laura drowns herself in the river rather than submit to a faith she cannot accept.
historical_context: 1896-98: the Catholic revival in the north of England, the Victorian debate on education and dogma, and the position of the old Catholic gentry.
literary_significance: Helbeck of Bannisdale is the finest of Ward's novels and one of the great English tragedies of religious difference: its portrait of an old Catholic family and its unsparing ending made it a critical favourite and it remains the most accomplished of her works.

title: Eleanor
description: Published in 1900 and Ward's most controversial novel: an American girl in Rome, torn between a career of religious scepticism and a Catholic lover.
plot_or_argument: Eleanor Burgoyne, a beautiful and clever American widow, is drawn to the Catholic Church by the aesthetics of Rome and by the love of a Catholic nobleman, but resists conversion; the novel follows her intellectual and emotional struggle, her friendship with a sceptical old priest's son, and her final choice of freedom.
historical_context: 1900: the American colony in Rome, the modernist crisis in the Catholic Church, and the debate over religious authority at the turn of the century.
literary_significance: Eleanor was Ward's most discussed late novel and one of the most intelligent treatments of religious choice in English fiction: it dramatises the conflict between the aesthetic appeal of Catholicism and the claims of intellectual freedom, and it shows her at the height of her powers as a novelist of ideas.

title: A Writer's Recollections
description: Published in 1918 and Ward's record of her Victorian literary life, her family and the making of Robert Elsmere.
plot_or_argument: Ward remembers her Tasmanian childhood, her father's conversion to Catholicism and return, her Oxford girlhood among the Arnolds, her friendship with George Eliot, the writing of Robert Elsmere and the storm it caused, and the settlement work of her middle years.
historical_context: 1917-18: the last year of the First World War, the retrospect of the Victorian age by one of its survivors, and the Arnold family history.
literary_significance: A Writer's Recollections is one of the most readable Victorian literary memoirs and a valuable record of the Arnold family, of George Eliot and of the crisis of faith that produced the greatest religious novel of the century.

title: King Solomon's Mines
description: Published in 1885 and the first great English adventure romance of Africa: Allan Quatermain's expedition into the interior in search of a lost civilisation and a legendary diamond mine.
plot_or_argument: Allan Quatermain, the hunter, is engaged by Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good to find Curtis's lost brother and the diamond mines of Solomon; the expedition crosses the desert, survives the mountains of Sheba, and reaches the lost Kukuana kingdom, where an Englishman is taken for a god and a civil war is fought before the treasure is found.
historical_context: 1885: the scramble for Africa, the discovery of the Zimbabwe ruins, the South African diamond fields, and the schoolboy market for adventure fiction.
literary_significance: King Solomon's Mines invented the modern adventure novel of Africa: its combination of documentary travel detail, a treasure hunt and an encounter with a lost civilisation set the formula for a century of imperial romance, and it made Haggard the most popular storyteller in England.

title: She: A History of Adventure
description: Published in 1887 and Haggard's masterpiece: the discovery of the immortal queen Ayesha in a lost city beneath an African volcano.
plot_or_argument: Leo Vincey and Horace Holly travel to the lost city of Kôr, where Ayesha, who has lived for two thousand years, believes Leo to be the reincarnation of her murdered lover Kallikrates; she bathes him in the flame of life, but the experiment that would make her mortal again destroys her, and the explorers escape the collapsing city.
historical_context: 1887: the archaeology of the ancient world, the Victorian interest in spiritualism and immortality, and the imperial exploration of central Africa.
literary_significance: She is one of the foundational books of modern popular fiction: Ayesha became one of the great mythic figures of English literature, the novel invented the lost-world romance that Conan Doyle, Kipling and the cinema would carry into the twentieth century, and it has never been out of print.

title: Allan Quatermain
description: Published in 1887 and the last adventure of Allan Quatermain: the ageing hunter's journey to a hidden white nation beyond the African lakes.
plot_or_argument: Quatermain, now rich and bored, sets out with Sir Henry Curtis and Captain Good to find the lost white race of the Zu-Vendi beyond the central lakes; they become involved in a dynastic war between two royal sisters, Quatermain is wounded, and the novel ends with his death and burial in Africa.
historical_context: 1887: the exploration of the African interior, the Victorian cult of the male adventure, and the market for sequels to a best-seller.
literary_significance: Allan Quatermain is the first great adventure sequel and the book that gave the imperial romance a hero capable of death: the passing of Quatermain made Haggard's protagonists mortal, an unusually serious touch in a popular genre, and it prepared the way for the more ambivalent imperial fiction of the 1890s.

title: Cleopatra
description: Published in 1889 and Haggard's great historical romance of the ancient world: the love of the Greek scholar Harmachis for the last queen of Egypt.
plot_or_argument: Harmachis, the heir of the priests and the destined liberator of Egypt, is sent into the palace at Alexandria to destroy Cleopatra, but falls under her spell; she betrays the conspiracy, he escapes to the desert, and returns years later to see the queen die by the asp before he dies himself.
historical_context: 1889: the Victorian fascination with Cleopatra, the archaeology of Egypt, and the imperial analogy between Rome and Britain.
literary_significance: Cleopatra is the finest of Haggard's historical romances and one of the great Victorian recreations of antiquity: its narrative of an Egyptian priest destroyed by the power of a queen made it a best-seller and it remains a landmark of the imperial historical romance.

title: Eric Brighteyes
description: Published in 1891 and Haggard's saga of the Viking age: the heroic life and death of an Icelandic warrior and his love for Gudruda the Fair.
plot_or_argument: Eric Brighteyes, the strongest and most generous of the Icelandic heroes, loves Gudruda the Fair but is ensnared by Swanhild, the witch-wife of his enemy Ospakar; the novel follows his outlawry, his voyages, his duel with Ospakar, and his death at the hands of Swanhild's magic.
historical_context: 1890-91: the Victorian enthusiasm for the Icelandic sagas, William Morris's and Eiríkur Magnússon's translations, and the imperial cult of northern courage.
literary_significance: Eric Brighteyes is the best of Haggard's historical novels and a remarkable English imitation of the Icelandic saga: its stern style and heroic fatalism made it a favourite of the saga revival and it stands at the head of the English tradition of Northern historical fiction.

title: The World's Desire
description: Published in 1890 and Haggard's collaboration with Andrew Lang: the wanderings of Odysseus, the last of the heroes, in search of Helen and the world's desire.
plot_or_argument: Odysseus, returned to Ithaca but unable to forget Helen, sets out again and comes to Egypt, where he meets the Queen Meriamun, who believes him to be her destined lover; he is imprisoned, escapes, and dies at last in the desert, while the gods take Helen away.
historical_context: 1889-90: the Victorian Homeric revival, Andrew Lang's anthropology and folklore, and the imperial reading of the Odyssey.
literary_significance: The World's Desire is one of the most interesting English continuations of Homer and a key text of the Victorian reimagining of the ancient world: its collaboration between a romancer and a scholar produced a strange and haunting book that influenced the later historical fantasy of the twentieth century.

title: Nada the Lily
description: Published in 1892 and Haggard's Zulu epic: the rise of a Zulu warrior in the time of Chaka and the tragedy of his love for Nada the Lily.
plot_or_argument: Umslopogaas, a Zulu warrior of royal blood, is raised in hiding from the tyrant Chaka; he becomes a chief, falls in love with Nada the Lily, and loses her to the jealousy of the witch-doctor, in a narrative of Zulu history told by Mopo, the old chief.
historical_context: 1891-92: the Zulu wars of the Victorian imagination, the ethnography of southern Africa, and Haggard's own South African service.
literary_significance: Nada the Lily is the most ambitious of Haggard's African romances and one of the few Victorian novels to give a sustained and sympathetic account of Zulu history: its narrative of Chaka's tyranny is a powerful and disturbing piece of historical fiction.

title: A Mummer's Wife
description: Published in 1885 and the first English naturalist novel: the destruction of a Midland draper's wife by the theatre, drink and desire.
plot_or_argument: Kate Ede, the wife of a consumptive draper in Hanley, falls in love with a travelling actor, leaves her husband and joins the touring company; the novel follows her years on the road, her husband's death, her decline into drink and her death in a London lodging-house, recorded with clinical flatness.
historical_context: 1884-85: the French naturalism of Zola and the Goncourts, the provincial theatre and the touring companies, and the circulating-library censorship of the 1880s.
literary_significance: A Mummer's Wife is the first English naturalist novel and a landmark of English fiction: its unsparing record of a woman's decline and its refusal to moralise or console introduced the Zola method into English and prepared the way for Gissing, Hardy and Moore's own Esther Waters.

title: Esther Waters
description: Published in 1894 and the finest English novel of domestic service: the life of a servant girl who bears an illegitimate child and fights to keep him.
plot_or_argument: Esther Waters, a kitchenmaid in a racing household, is seduced by the footman William Latch, loses her place when she is pregnant, and raises her son alone through years of service in London and the south coast; she refuses marriage to a good man rather than give up her child, and the novel ends with her back in service and her son a bookmaker.
historical_context: 1894: the servant question, the racing world, the workhouse and the lying-in hospital, and the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts.
literary_significance: Esther Waters is the classic English novel of the servant and one of the greatest novels of the 1890s: its patient, unsentimental record of a working woman's life has been recognised as the English masterpiece of naturalism, and it remains the finest fictional account of domestic service in the language.

title: A Drama in Muslin
description: Published in 1886 and Moore's Irish novel of the marriage market: a group of girls brought out in Dublin to find husbands.
plot_or_argument: Alice Barton and her friends are brought from their convent school to the Dublin season of balls and garden parties, where the girls are sold to the highest bidder; Alice, plain and clever, escapes into a marriage with a Dublin doctor and a life of social conscience, while her friend Cecilia is destroyed by the marriage market.
historical_context: 1885-86: the Irish landed class in decline, the Dublin Castle season, the Land League agitation, and the Victorian debate on women's education.
literary_significance: A Drama in Muslin is the strongest Irish novel of the 1880s and one of the most astringent treatments of the marriage market in English: its picture of the Dublin season and of the destruction of women by the marriage system made it a key text of the New Woman debate and it was banned by the circulating libraries.

title: Confessions of a Young Man
description: Published in 1888 and the most scandalous memoir of the Aesthetic movement: Moore's account of his years among the painters and poets of Paris.
plot_or_argument: Moore recalls his Irish boyhood, his escape to Paris in 1873, his study of painting and his meetings with Manet, Degas, Zola and the Impressionists, his return to London, his discovery of Wagner and his adoption of the Decadent creed of art for art's sake.
historical_context: 1873-88: the Paris of the Impressionists, the literary Bohemia of London in the 1880s, and the aesthetic movement's cult of the self.
literary_significance: Confessions of a Young Man is the liveliest English document of the Aesthetic movement and one of the most influential autobiographies of the century: its brilliant, insolent prose made Decadence a literary programme in English and it gave the movement its most quotable memoir.

title: The Untilled Field
description: Published in 1903 and the founding book of the modern Irish short story: fifteen stories of priest-ridden rural Ireland.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow the parishioners and priests of a Mayo village through emigration, clerical tyranny, the failure of love and the small cruelties of village life, and end with the departure of the young for America.
historical_context: 1899-1902: the Irish Literary Revival, the land agitation and emigration of the 1890s, and the foundation of the Irish Literary Theatre.
literary_significance: The Untilled Field invented the modern Irish short story and gave the Irish Revival its most exact prose: its influence on Joyce, O'Connor and the Irish story is direct and acknowledged, and it is the first work in which Moore's Irish subject matter found its proper form.

title: Children of the Ghetto
description: Published in 1892 and the first great English novel of the Jewish East End: a year in the life of the immigrant community of London.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows the Ansell family and their neighbours through the synagogue, the workshop, the Board School and the pawnshop: Reb Shemuel's daughter Esther is torn between the old faith and a modern marriage, the rebellious son disappears into the world, and the community's poverty, piety and humour are recorded in a series of connected scenes.
historical_context: 1891-92: the mass immigration of Russian and Polish Jews after 1881, the Whitechapel ghetto, the Jews' Free School, and the debate on anglicisation.
literary_significance: Children of the Ghetto was the first English novel to give the Jewish immigrant community a full literary existence: it made Zangwill famous as the 'Dickens of the Ghetto', it recorded the speech and customs of the East End before they vanished, and it stands at the head of the English-Jewish tradition.

title: The King of Schnorrers
description: Published in 1894 and Zangwill's comic masterpiece: the exploits of Manasseh Bueno Barzillai Azevedo da Costa, the proudest beggar in eighteenth-century London.
plot_or_argument: Manasseh, a Sephardi schnorrer of immense dignity, lives by extracting alms from the rich of Bevis Marks; he outwits a wealthy Ashkenazi on the point of honour, tricks a merchant into supporting his daughter's wedding, and defeats every attempt to humiliate him, in a picaresque comedy of the Jewish community of 1780.
historical_context: 1780s: the Sephardi and Ashkenazi communities of London, the Bevis Marks synagogue, and the Yiddish comic tradition of the schlemiel and the schnorrer.
literary_significance: The King of Schnorrers is a comic classic and the first English book to draw on the Yiddish humour of the immigrant world: its portrait of Manasseh is one of the great comic creations in English fiction and it opened the way for the Jewish-American humour of the next century.

title: Dreamers of the Ghetto
description: Published in 1898 and Zangwill's gallery of Jewish lives: a series of imagined portraits of figures from Spinoza to Heine.
plot_or_argument: The volume presents episodes in the lives of Spinoza, Sabbatai Zevi, Uriel Acosta, Heine, Lassalle, and a company of modern dreamers, each caught at the moment when the vision of the ghetto meets the world outside it.
historical_context: 1897-98: the Zionist movement after the first Congress of 1897, the Jewish Enlightenment, and the debate over assimilation and national identity.
literary_significance: Dreamers of the Ghetto is the most ambitious of Zangwill's books and a key text of the early Zionist imagination: its portraits of the great Jewish heretics and dreamers gave the movement a gallery of heroic ancestors and it remains a striking experiment in the historical portrait.

title: The Melting Pot
description: First performed in 1908 and the play that gave the language its phrase: the love of a Russian-Jewish immigrant and a Christian girl in New York, and the vision of America as the crucible of the races.
plot_or_argument: David Quixano, a composer who survived the Kishinev pogrom, writes an American symphony in a New York settlement house; he falls in love with Vera, the daughter of the Russian baron who commanded the pogrom, and in the last act the two are united in a vision of the great melting pot in which all races are fused into a new American.
historical_context: 1908: the mass immigration through Ellis Island, the settlement houses of New York, the Kishinev pogrom of 1903, and the American debate on assimilation.
literary_significance: The Melting Pot gave the English language its most enduring metaphor for American immigrant assimilation: the play was a sensation in the United States and its title became the standard term for the American fusion of peoples, making Zangwill one of the most influential writers on the idea of America.
